back: A model of $P(w_1,\dots,w_m)$, factorised by the chain rule into next-word predictions $P(w_i\mid w_{<i})$.
So the model learns sentence starts and ends and the chain rule covers the first word and the stopping decision.
Unseen n-grams get probability 0, so a sentence containing one gets 0 and perplexity infinity; solved by smoothing.
$P=\frac{c(v,w)+k}{c(v)+k|V|}$. With k=1 (Laplace) it takes too much mass from seen events on large vocabularies.
$\lambda P_{n}+(1-\lambda)P_{n-1}$ mixes orders; tune $\lambda$ on held-out data.
Use the highest-order estimate with positive count; otherwise fall back to a lower order (Katz discounts to keep normalisation; stupid backoff just multiplies by ~0.4).
Lower-order probability should reflect in how many different contexts a word appears, not its raw frequency (Francisco almost only follows San).
The effective branching factor: a uniform choice among $b$ words has perplexity $b$. Lower is better.
Only comparable with the same vocabulary and tokenisation; needs unseen test data; infinite if any probability is 0.
Up to $|V|^n$ cells; most are empty, which is why counts get sparse as n grows.

front: Idea of a neural language model
back: Embed the previous words, pass through a network, softmax over the vocabulary; similar words share statistics, no smoothing needed.

front: Link between LM loss and perplexity
back: Training minimises the average cross-entropy $H$; perplexity is $e^{H}$ (or $2^{H}$ with bits).
